event: Saturday of week five: the Fell Cup. Bea is up at five, white-faced, and eats one dry toast.
You make her breathe out, twice. She holds your ringed hand. "Jetty wall," she says. "Shouting."
At eight she goes down to the boathouse with Morwenna and the four; at the door she turns and waves.
The morning is cold and still, the mere like glass, frost on the reeds, a thin mist lifting.
By half past nine half the academy lines the shore path, in scarves, with flasks and banners.
Shiv unrolls her bedsheet on the path: green paint, Irish words, a drawing of a rude oar. Cheers.
"What does it say?" you ask. Shiv grins. "Thornfield. Row. And something about Ashcombe's mothers."
Kit arrives in an Ashcombe scarf, takes it off in front of the Ashcombe girls, and stands with you.
"Traitor," someone shouts. Kit, scarlet, shouts back: "Thornfield!" and nearly dies of it.
Lin has her sketchbook; Priya and Amara share a flask; Yusra stands at the back, off duty, watching.
You walk on with Kit and Lin along the shore to the village jetty wall, to wait at the finish.
The village crowds the wall: old women, girls, a dog in a scarf, the shopkeeper with a bell.
On a table by the jetty sits the Fell Cup: old dented pewter, polished, on a folded tea towel.
At ten, far down the mere, a flag drops. A faint shout. Five boats leap forward, small as insects.
For a long minute they're just specks; then the colours come clear: green for Thornfield.
Ashcombe's blue boat is ahead from the start, smooth and fast; Thornfield's third, then second.
"Come on," Kit says, gripping your arm. "Come on, come on." Lin has stopped drawing.
The boats reach the bend by the reeds. Ashcombe leads by a length. You think of Bea's hand: BEND.
Thornfield's stroke rate goes up. You see it from the wall: the oars quicker, all together.
Ashcombe fades at the bend, the way Morwenna said they always do; the green boat closes on them.
You're shouting before you know it: Bea's name, over and over, hoarse.
Shiv's voice comes down the shore, howling in Irish; Kit is shouting "Thornfield!" beside you.
The last two hundred yards: Thornfield and Ashcombe level, the other three falling back.
You can see Bea now at bow, her face screwed up, her hair coming loose, pulling with everything.
The jetty wall roars. The shopkeeper rings her bell like a madwoman. The dog barks.
Thornfield crosses the line a third of a length ahead. The umpire's flag goes up: green.
For a second there's silence on the wall. Then everyone from Thornfield screams at once.
Thornfield's first Fell Cup since 1987. Kit is hugging you, and Lin, and a stranger, and crying.
Out on the water Bea collapses over her oar; then she sits up and looks for the jetty wall.
She finds you. She lifts one arm, shaking, and points straight at you. You wave both arms back.
The four rows in to the jetty; Bea climbs out soaked, staggers, and walks straight into your arms.
"Did you see?" Bea says into your neck. "BEND. I heard you. I heard you all the way."
She kisses you, wet and laughing, in front of the whole village and half the academy; they cheer.
Morwenna lifts the dented pewter cup over her head on the jetty, booming, and hands it to Bea.
Bea holds it up, crying and laughing; the whole wall cheers; Shiv's bedsheet waves on the path.
Lin draws Bea holding up the cup, fast, three lines; she tears it out and gives it to her.
Yusra comes to the edge of the crowd. She shakes Bea's hand. "Lindqvist," she says. "Good."
Bea, astonished, hugs her; Yusra stands it, stiff, then laughs, and pats Bea's soaking back.
Yusra looks at you over Bea's shoulder. "Front door," she says. "When you're ready. No rush."
The four carry the boat back to the boathouse in a crowd of singing girls; Bea rides on the cheer.
By noon Bea is in a hot bath with the cup on the windowsill, singing; she sends you off with a wave.
"Go," she shouts through the door. "Walk with your warden. I've won a cup. I'm a legend now."
Yusra is at the Thornfield front door at half past twelve, in her boots, with the rucksack.
"Not the fell today," she says. "The shore. The far side. It's quiet there." You walk.
Round the mere, away from the noise; the path through the alders, the water bright between trees.
Yusra holds your hand as soon as the academy is out of sight. She says: "That was a good race."
"You shouted," you say. Yusra looks offended. "I did not." Then: "Once. Maybe twice."
On the far shore there's a fallen oak by the water; you sit on it; she unpacks tea and sandwiches.
She sees the ring on your finger, and lifts your hand, and turns it to the light. "Kit's work?"
You say yes; a focus. Yusra looks at the inward hook a long moment. "It knows you," she says.
"Everyone's giving you things," she says. "I've got nothing. Tea." You say tea is a ward, she said.
Yusra laughs, really laughs. Then she kisses you, there on the oak, slow, her hand at your jaw.
It's longer than on the fell; warmer; less afraid. When she pulls back she's smiling properly.
"I slept seven hours last night," Yusra says. "Whole nights, off shift. That's you. Partly."
She leans on you, and you sit by the bright water till the sun starts down and the cold comes.
At the alders she lets go of your hand, and is your warden again; her eyes stay soft all the way.
Evening: the Drowned Bell, all of Thornfield packed in, the cup on the bar full of cider.
Bea is lifted onto a table and made to make a speech; she says "BEND!" and falls off into arms.
Kit buys a round with money she says she was saving. Shiv sings; Lin draws; Priya cries.
Bea finds you at the bar, pink and sweaty and delirious. "Take me home," she says. "Now. Please."
In 15 she shuts the door and pushes you against it, laughing, kissing you hard and greedy.
"I won a fucking cup," Bea says against your mouth. "I want you. Now. Everything." You laugh.
She strips your jumper off; you strip hers; she pulls you down onto the rug in the lamplight.
You get her leggings off and she's bare and soaked already; you put your mouth on her small tits.
"Fuck me," Bea says, gripping your hair. "Please. I'm so wet. I've been wet since the jetty."
You push two fingers into her cunt and fuck her hard and slow on the rug; she moans your name.
She rides your hand, gasping, her blistered hands on your shoulders, her hips working.
She comes loud, shaking, laughing; then flips you over and buries her face between your legs.
She licks your cunt like she's starving, her tongue on your clit, two fingers deep inside you.
You come hard, crying out, your thighs shaking round her head; Bea laughs into you, delighted.
After, you lie tangled on the rug, sweaty, the cup gleaming on the windowsill above you.
"Thornfield," Bea tells the ceiling. "Nineteen eighty-seven. And me." You both laugh till you ache.
You carry the blanket down to the rug and sleep there, tangled, her hand on your ringed hand.
A day at Hollowmere ends.
